newsitem.title: USA: Rubin declines comment on forex levels.
newsitem.headline: Rubin declines comment on forex levels.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Friday declined to comment on specific exchange rates but defended U.S. dollary policy as good for the economy and referred to recent Group of Seven and Japanese concerns about currency movements.
Rubin, in Williamsburg, Va., to speak to a meeting of the Business Council, was asked by CNBC business television what he would tell company executives who told him the dollar was too strong.

"I'm going to tell them what I always tell them. ... I think our dollar policy has been right. I think it has contributed to lower interest rates, I think that it has contributed to confidence in our markets and I think it has contributed to lower inflation," he said.

"Having said that, I'm going to remind them of the recent statement by G7 finance ministers and central bank governors, which as you know issued a communique about two weeks ago, saying that it was very important that exchange rates not get out of synch with economic fundamentals," Rubin said.
"Then I will also remind them that the Japanese government officials have recently expressed concern about movements in the yen and we have agreed with their concerns," he said.
"You put all that together and I think you get both our dollar policy and a set of exchange rate views of economic officials around the world."
Rubin declined to comment on whether current exchange rates reflected economic fundamentals. "I never comment on the specifics of particular exchange rates but that is the policy framework."
Rubin also declined to comment on dollar/yen levels when asked by reporters about Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara's suggestion that the dollar could drop to 103 yen.
"I wouldn't express a view of where it might go or what it might do," Rubin said.
"I would just say we share their (Japanese) concerns about recent movements in the context of the G7."
On the U.S. economy, Rubin said that the general view among economists is that the 5.6 percent growth rate seen in the first quarter was above a sustainable level.
"Whatever the fluctuation might be from quarter to quarter, we really are on a most likely path of continued solid growth," Rubin said.
Rubin was upbeat about the 2002 balanced budget agreement reached between the Clinton Administration and the Republican-controlled Congress.
"I think we'll get this together," Rubin said of the work being done to flesh out last week's agreement.
"We still have to work out the final details," Rubin said, noting it was an agreement that was based on a number of agreements and understandings.

Rubin echoed comments of his deputy, Lawrence Summers, that the May 7 effective date for any capital gains tax cut, as announced by the top Republican tax writers, was appropriate. "It think that was a sensible judgment on their part."
